subject: Biology
title: Ocean Plastic Pollution
description: A micro-lesson that makes Ocean Plastic Pollution usable.

hook.text: There are an estimated 5 trillion pieces of plastic floating in the world's oceans right now.

buildup.text: Plastic doesn't biodegrade. It breaks into microplastics—tiny fragments that enter every level of the food chain.

discovery.text: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is a swirling mass of debris twice the size of Texas.

twist.text: Microplastics have been found in human blood, breast milk, and placentas. We're consuming our own waste.

climax.text: Over a million seabirds and 100,000 marine mammals die from plastic entanglement or ingestion each year.

punchline.text: We made plastic last forever. Now it's everywhere.

quiz.question: How many pieces of plastic are estimated to be in the ocean?

details.summary: Over 8 million metric tons of plastic enter the oceans annually, breaking into microplastics that pervade every marine environment from surface to seafloor. Marine animals ingest plastic or become entangled, and microplastics have been found in the deepest ocean trenches.
details.whyItMatters: Plastic pollution threatens marine ecosystems from individual organisms to entire food webs. Microplastics entering the food chain raise concerns about human health through seafood consumption and drinking water contamination.
takeaways: Over 8 million metric tons of plastic enter the ocean each year
Microplastics have been found in the Mariana Trench and Arctic sea ice
Over 700 marine species are known to interact with plastic debris

faq.question: What happens to plastic in the ocean?
faq.answer: Sunlight, waves, and salt break plastic into smaller and smaller pieces called microplastics but never fully decompose it. These fragments concentrate persistent organic pollutants on their surfaces and are ingested by organisms at every level of the food web.

faq.question: Can ocean plastic pollution be cleaned up?
faq.answer: Large floating debris can be collected, but microplastics dispersed throughout the water column and sediments are essentially impossible to remove. Prevention through reducing plastic production and improving waste management is far more effective than cleanup.
